content.title: About
content.content: Soup and broth are liquid dishes obtained by simmering meat, fish, poultry, vegetables, or a combination thereof. They serve as a flavorful base for many recipes, providing aroma, nutrients, and a warming effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of making broths dates back several millennia and appears in cultures from ancient China to medieval Europe.
In 1905 Russia began mass‑producing bone broths for therapeutic diets, calling them "liquid gold".
Broths can be clear (classic) or thick (e.g., cream soups), depending on the thickening method used.
Classic French consommé is clarified by removing fat and impurities through a filtration process.
Soups are often served with garnishes such as noodles, rice, grains, or fresh herbs.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Bone broths contain gelatin, which converts to collagen during digestion, supporting joint and skin health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Simmering bones and vegetables releases calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, essential for bones and nerve function.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Soups are mostly water, helping maintain the body's fluid balance.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Warm liquid foods are digested quickly, making them beneficial during colds or post‑surgery recovery.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Contains amino acids (glycine, proline) that contribute to the synthesis of immune proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared soups are often salted; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Contamination if stored improperly
items.content: Broth left at room temperature for more than 2 hours can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Soups based on seafood or dairy may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Excess saturated fat
items.content: Broths made from fatty cuts of meat can contain high levels of saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve soups hot, often with herbs, spices, noodles, rice, or vegetable pieces. They can be enjoyed on their own or used as a base for more complex dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the broth to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before consumption.
